subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: “Five minutes, Mummy, just five minutes!” Kishore called, crayon already moving over the paper. The school bus came at 7:40, and it was 7:25. His mother Swati kept an eye on the clock while she packed the tiffin. The sun took three minutes. Then the mountains needed a river, and the river needed a boat with a flag, and the flag needed all the colours. At 7:38 the bus honked. Kishore looked up, astonished. “Already?” he said, and meant it. He grabbed the drawing, still wet in the corners, stuffed his shoes on the wrong feet and ran down the stairs with the picture smudging against his shirt.

qa.q: What time did the school bus come?
qa.a: The school bus came at 7:40.

qa.q: Why was Kishore astonished when the bus honked?
qa.a: Kishore sincerely believed only five minutes had passed and felt surprised and a little shocked that the time had run out so soon.

qa.q: What could Kishore and Swati try tomorrow so the drawing does not collide with the bus?
qa.a: Set a timer for the drawing, or start earlier, and decide which part gets finished before the bus.

qa.q: How might Swati feel watching the clock while packing the tiffin?
qa.a: Swati is likely anxious about the bus and patient with Kishore at once, since the promise of “five minutes” was sincere but unreliable.

grounding: A child promises a drawing will take five minutes and is surprised by how much time has gone.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Tenzin sat on the sofa with a football in hand. “You said five minutes,” Tenzin said. Mridul didn't look up from his block castle. “Five minutes,” he agreed. The clock over the door said 4:10. Mridul added a bridge, then a tower, then a gate that opened. He was sure he had only just begun. At 5:05 Tenzin put the football down, said “I'll go down to the park with Kabir,” and left. Mridul glanced at the clock and frowned. “That was quick,” he said to the empty room. Through the window he could see two small figures on the grass, already kicking the ball, and the castle suddenly looked smaller.

qa.q: What time did the clock over the door show when Tenzin was waiting?
qa.a: The clock over the door said 4:10.

qa.q: What did Mridul feel when he saw the clock at 5:05?
qa.a: Mridul felt surprised and frowned, because to him the time seemed to have passed so quickly; his “That was quick” shows the promise of five minutes was sincere.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next time before promising Tenzin a time?
qa.a: Look at the clock when starting, guess how long the castle will really take, and tell Tenzin an honest time or stop at a set hour.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after waiting almost an hour?
qa.a: Tenzin is probably disappointed and a bit annoyed at waiting, yet still wants to play, so leaves for the park with Kabir.

grounding: A child promises five minutes and loses an hour, with little felt sense of duration.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: My name is Varun. Last Sunday, my cousin Damini asked if I could come fly kites. I said, "Wait, I just have to finish my dinosaur drawing. Five minutes!" I really thought so. I had the outline done already. Then I started the scales. Each scale needed a little shadow. Then the tail needed spikes, and the sky needed clouds. When I looked up, the clock said four. I had started at three. Damini was sitting on the steps, bored, and her kite was still rolled up. I felt shocked. Where did the hour go? Now I say, "Maybe an hour," and I'm usually right.

qa.q: What was Varun drawing?
qa.a: Varun was drawing a dinosaur.

qa.q: How did Varun feel on seeing the clock said four?
qa.a: Varun felt shocked, genuinely surprised that an hour had gone when five minutes had seemed true.

qa.q: What small change did Varun make afterwards?
qa.a: Varun now says "Maybe an hour" instead of five minutes, which is usually right.

qa.q: What was it like for Damini to wait?
qa.a: Damini sat on the steps, bored, with her kite still rolled up, waiting for a promise that turned out to be far too short.

grounding: A child promises a drawing will take five minutes and is surprised when an hour has gone.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Teacher's note, Class 3 art period, Monday.
Neelam told me at the start that her clay pot would take "two minutes" and she would then help Abhinav with his. She meant it completely. She shaped the base, then decided it needed a handle, then a pattern of dots. At the bell, forty minutes later, she looked up amazed. "It's over already?" Abhinav had waited, then finished alone. I showed Neelam the wall clock and where the big hand had been when she began. Tomorrow I will try a sand timer on her table so she can see time moving while she works.

qa.q: What did Neelam say at the start about the clay pot?
qa.a: She said her clay pot would take "two minutes".

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when the bell rang?
qa.a: She was amazed and surprised that forty minutes had gone, since she had meant her two-minute promise completely.

qa.q: What does the note-writer plan to try, and why could it help?
qa.a: A sand timer on Neelam's table, so she can actually see time passing while she works.

qa.q: How was Abhinav affected by Neelam's estimate?
qa.a: Abhinav waited for the promised help and then had to finish alone, perhaps feeling a little let down.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child sincerely underestimating how long a task will take.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Manjula didi asked me to watch the rice on the stove while she went to the shop. I said I'd finish my block castle first, "super quick." I only needed the tower. But then the drawbridge fell off, and I had to fix it, and then I made a flag. When didi came back, the rice smelled burnt and the stove was still on. She switched it off fast. She wasn't angry, just tired. I felt terrible. I thought only a few minutes had gone. Didi says next time I should set the kitchen timer. I will. 😔
Suraj

qa.q: What was Suraj building?
qa.a: Suraj was building a castle, finishing the tower.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when didi came back?
qa.a: Suraj felt terrible and guilty, having thought only a few minutes had gone while the rice burnt.

qa.q: What could Suraj do next time?
qa.a: Suraj could set the kitchen timer, as didi suggested, or leave the castle until the rice is done.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula didi to come home to burnt rice?
qa.a: Manjula didi seems tired rather than angry, and has to switch the stove off quickly and suggest a timer.

grounding: A child's diary shows a sincere promise of 'super quick' turning into a much longer time than expected.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
On the day of the Diwali mela in Kudal village, Parveen sat on the courtyard floor with a lump of clay. "One diya for Ammi. Five minutes," she told Tenzin, already in his new shirt.
"The bus goes at four."
"Five minutes."
The clay cracked. She wet it and started again. The spout fell over. She scratched a pattern with a twig, rubbed it off because it was crooked, and did it again.
Tenzin waited on the step, walked to the gate and back, and waited again.
When Parveen held up a small, lopsided diya, the shadows had crossed the courtyard. A bell in the next village rang five.
"Five minutes?" Tenzin said.
Parveen's mouth fell open. "But… it was only five minutes!"

qa.q: At what time did the bus go?
qa.a: The bus goes at four.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when she heard the bell ring five?
qa.a: Parveen felt shocked and surprised, sure it had only been five minutes.

qa.q: What could help Parveen next time she says "five minutes"?
qa.a: Parveen could ask a grown-up to set a timer or check the clock, since it is hard to feel how long making something really takes.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel while waiting?
qa.a: Tenzin was impatient and restless, walking to the gate and back while the time for the bus passed.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sincerely promises a clay diya will take five minutes and is surprised when more than an hour has gone.
